parties:
Hamida Real Estate Construction Ltd and another ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili) and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2. The plaintiffs, Hamida Real Estate Ltd and Nasrul Hamid filed Title Suit No. 407 of 2005 in the First Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka for cancellation of Power of Attorney dated 10-8-2005 executed by the defendant No.1, Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili), as void, illegal, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff petitioner No.2, Nasrul Hamid, and also for further decree that the Power of Attorney executed by the defendant-opposite party No. 1, Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili) in favour of the plaintiff petitioner No.2, Nasrul Hamid, on 43-7-1998 as legal, operative and irrevocable and also binding upon the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 and also for mandatory and permanent injunction against the defendant-opposite parties Nos. 1 and 2 Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili), and RAJUK. 

 3. The case of the plaintiffs, in short, is that one Nurul Huda Khandaker obtained lease of 15 kathas 8 chhataks under plot No. CWN(A)4 on 3-11-1965 from the then DIT; that Nurul Huda sold out the same in favour of the father of the defendant-opposite party No.1, Shahjahan, on 31-5-1969 and he mutated his name with the then DlT and upon obtaining approval of plan he constructed a 2(two) storied building thereon; that Shahjahan orally gifted the property in favour of his wife, Hasina Begum, and daughter, defendant-opposite party No.1, Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili), and confirmed' the same by affidavit sworn on 21-1-1975 before the Magistrate, First Class, Dhaka and that they subsequently mutated their names. 

 4. It is further stated that subsequently on an amicable partition, the front portion of the said plot fell in the saham of the defendant-opposite party No. 1, Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili), and she had been possessing the same; that subsequently Hasina Begum again gifted the said property in favour of her husband, Shahjahan; that Shahjahan died on 7-4-1992 and his share was inherited by the defendant-opposite party No. 1, Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili), and the two brothers of Shahjahan namely Altaf Hossain and Fazle Hossain and sister Latifun Nessa but they relinquished their claim over the suit land in favour of the defendant-opposite party No.1, Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili), in exchange of other property of Shahjahan at 3/11, Johnson Road, Sutrapur, Dhaka. 

 5. It is also stated that the defendant-opposite party No. 1, Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili), entered into an agreement for sale with the plaintiff-petitioner No. 1 Hamida Real Estate Construction Ltd on 27- 12-1994 to sell the properties described in the plaint at a consideration of Taka 1,35,94,800 and received an amount of Taka 5,00,000 as earnest money; that the defendant-opposite party No. 1, Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili), received an amount of Taka 15,00,000 on 23-2-1995 and thereafter handed over possession of the suit property in favour of the plaintiff- petitioner No. 1 Hamida Real Estate Construction Ltd and since the plaintiff-petitioner No.1. Hamida Real Estate Construction Ltd. has been possessing the property by leasing out the same to Standard Bank, Gulshan Branch, Dhaka. Pursuant to the deed of agreement of sale permission was sought for by the defendant-opposite" party No. I from RAJUK for transfer of the said suit land in favour of the plaintiff-petitioner No. 1. 

 6. It is further stated that the defendant-opposite party No.1, Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili), subsequently on several occasions, upon executing acknowledgement receipts, received further amount of Taka 1,54,90,00 against the sale of the suit property; that in spite of receiving of more than the consideration amount the defendant-opposite party No. 1, Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili), did not execute and register the sale deed and at one stage the defendant-opposite party No.1, Malika. Hasina Jahan (Lili) executed an Irrevocable Power of Attorney on 23-7-1998 appointing the plaintiff-petitioner No.2, Nasrul Hamid, as her Attorney authorising him to take necessary steps in respect of transfer of the suit land and handed over all original documents to him; that the power of attorney in favour of the plaintiff-petitioner No. 1 was approved by RAJUK on 21-12-2000 and in such process, the plaintiff-petitioner No. 1 spent more than Taka 78,00,000 and the defendant-opposite party No. 1, Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili), acknowledged the same by putting her own signature as witness No. 1 to a memorandum of understanding on 2-3-2005; that in such circumstances, the power of Attorney dated 23-7-1998 has been acted upon and the defendant-opposite party No. 1, Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili) is bound by the actions taken by the plaintiff- petitioner No.1, Nasrul Hamid, under the power of attorney; that petitioner No.2, Nasrul Hamid, executed a Baina Nama for transfer of the suit land pursuant to the power of attorney in favour of the proforma defendant-opposite party No.4, Hamida Soater Limited on 20-5-2005 at a consideration of Taka 2,57,01,000 and that thereafter sought permission before the RAJUK for transfer of the suit land in favour of the proforma opposite party No.4. 

 7. It is further stated that the plaintiff-petitioners came to learn that the defendant-opposite party No.1, Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili), has been trying to do some misdeeds with regard to the transfer of the suit land and all on a sudden on 14-8-2005 handed over the deed of cancellation of power of attorney on 14-8-2004 executed by the defendant- opposite party No. 1, Malika Hasina Jahana (Lili), canceling the power of attorney dated 23-7-1998 and suppressed all the aforementioned transactions and facts and circumstances of the case. 

 8. It is also stated that the defendant-opposite party No.1, Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili), again has been demanding an amount of Taka 1,00,00,000 from the plaintiffs-petitioners for cancellation or revocation of the said cancellation of the power of Attorney dated 10-8-2005. The further case of the plaintiff is that in the aforesaid facts and circumstances, the defendant-opposite party No. 1, Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili) has been trying to deny the agreement dated 27-12-1994, power of attorney dated 23-7-1998 and transaction of consideration against the said deed of agreement and other monetary transactions between the defendant-opposite party No.1, and the plaintiffs-petitioners and in such circumstances, the plaintiffs-petitioners served legal notice upon the defendants opposite parties and filed the said suit making the aforesaid prayers. The defendant-opposite party No. 1 appeared in the suit and had been contesting the same by filing written statement. 

 12. The defendant No.1, Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili), filed Civil Revision No. 21 of 2006 in the court of the learned District Judge, Dhaka under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure against the order dated 3-1-2006 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Dhaka in the said Title Suit No. 407 of 2005 and prayed for stay operation of the order dated 3-1-2006 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Dhaka. 

 16. The plaintiffs-petitioners filed another application on 1-2-2006 for dismissal of the Civil Revision on the ground of maintainability stating amongst others, that the learned District Judge has no pecuniary jurisdiction to adjudicate the Civil Revision the valuation of which is Taka 2,57,01,000 which exceeds the pecuniary jurisdiction of the learned District Judge given under section 6 and 15(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 21 (1) of the Civil Court's Act and also on the ground that the order allowing temporary injunction under Order XXXIX, rule 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure is an appealable order and not revisable, as such, the civil revision filed against the order of temporary injunction is not maintainable. 

 20. The learned Additional District Judge, 7th Court, Dhaka without adjourning hearing of the Civil Revision and application of dismissing the Civil Revision, heard the Civil Revision and by judgment and order dated 29-3-2006 allowed the Civil Revision and thereby allowed the application filed by the defendant-opposite party No.1, Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili), under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure and thus rejected the plaint. 

 21. Mr Ozair Farooq, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, submits that the learned Additional District Judge heard and disposed of the Civil Revision valued at Taka 2,57,01,000 which is beyond his pecuniary jurisdiction and, as such, he cannot allow the revisional application without taking into consideration that the Civil Revision is not maintainable and prayed for setting aside the order of the learned Additional District Judge. 

 22. The opposite party No.1, Malika Hasina Jahan (Lili), by filing a counter-affidavit denied all the material allegations stated by the defendant. Mr Abdul Quyaums the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party No.1 submits that the revisional application was filed on 19-1-2006 and the judgment passed in Civil Revision No. 1701 of 2005 on 8-2-2006 has not decided about pending case before the learned District Judge. So, in view of the decision of the larger Bench, the jurisdiction of the District Judge in pending case was not taken away. He further submits that the court below rightly passed the impugned order, which must be upheld. 

 24. For determining the question as to whether the learned District Judge or Additional District Judge has jurisdiction to hear and dispose of revisional application of value exceeding 5,00,000, we may profitably refer some portion of decision of our larger Bench which has been reported in 58 DLR 211 in the following lines: 

 "115 Revision (1) The High Court Division may on the application of any party aggrieved: call for the record of any suit or proceeding, in which a decree or an order has been passed by a court of District Judge or Additional District Judge, or decree has been passed by a court of Joint District Judge, Senior Assistant Judge or  Assistant Judge from which no appeal lies; and if such Court appears to have committed any error of law resulting in an error in such decree or order occasioning failure of justice, the High Court Division may revise such decree or order and, make such order in the suit or proceeding . as it thinks fit. 

 (2) The Court of District Judge may, on the application of any party aggrieved, call for the record of any suit or proceeding in which an order has been. passed by a court of Joint District Judge, Senior Assistant Judge or Assistant Judge from which no appeal lies and if such court appears to have committed any error of law resulting in an error in such order occasioning failure of justice, the court of District Judge may revise such order and make such order as it thinks fit." 

 26. Section 19. Extent of Jurisdiction of Senior Assistant Judge etc. Save as other i e provided by any enactment for the time being in force, the juridiction of a Senior Assistant Judge and Assistant Judge shall extend to all suits of which the value does not exceed four lac taka and two lac taka respectively. 

 (a) to the District Judge where the value of the original suit in which or in any proceeding arising out of which the decree or order was made did not exceed five lac, and 

 28. Section 19 of the Civil Courts Act provides for the pecuniary jurisdiction of Senior Assistant Judge and Assistant Judge in respect of suit, Sub-section 2 of section 21 indicate that an appeal shall lie to the district Judge again to decree order passed by the Senior Assistant Judge or Assistant Judge. Order as employed in sub-section (2) implies appealable order as, contemplated under Order XLIII, rule (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure or any order passed in any proceedings like preemption proceeding, suits or proceedings of which the value exceeds four lac taka will lie to the Joint District Judge having unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction. But according to the provision of sub-section (1) of section 21, appeal from a decree or order passed by the Joint District Judge will lie to the District Judge, in which the value of the original suit or proceeding did not exceed take five lac. Therefore, in a suit filed before the Joint District Judge the value of which does not exceed five lac taka, if a decree or order as the case' may be, is passed appeal will lie to the District Judge. As per clause (b) of sub-section 1 of section 21, appeal will lie to the High Court Division in any other cases i.e. when the value exceeds Taka five lac. 

 30. Section 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure as we have already noted, indicates the pecuniary jurisdiction of any court over suits. Therefore, the pecuniary value will determine the forum and the jurisdiction over the subject matter of the proceedings in the civil jurisdiction. Importantly, section 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure is inextricably linked to section 8 of the Suits Valuation Act, 1887 which is as under: 

 " 8. Court fee value and jurisdiction value to be the same in certain suits-Where the suits other than those referred to the Court Fees Act, 1870 (VII of 1870) section 7, Paragraphs (v)(vi) and (ix) an paragraphs (x) claus (d), Court Fees are payable advalorem under the court fees Act, 1870 the value as determinable for the computation of court fees and the value for purpose of jurisdiction shall be same." 

 31. The above provision indicates that the value for the purpose of jurisdiction and court fees should be same. 

 32. With advantage, we may also refer to section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act, 1887 where provisions have been made in respect of procedure where objection is taken on appeal or revision that a suit or appeal was not properly valued for jurisdictional purposes. And it is indicated there that the objection as to the valuation for jurisdictional purposes shall be taken at the first instance, and such objection as regards valuation for jurisdiction purpose can also be taken in revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 33. Reading section 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure and sections 8 and II of the Suits Valuation Act and the relevant provisions of the Civil Courts Act as stated above the conclusion would follow that the value of the suit or proceeding would conclusively determine the forum where suits Of proceeding will be filed and tried and the appeal will be heard and disposed of. Thus the forum of appeal is to be determined according to the value of the suit or proceeding and the value of appeal consequently will lead to the revisional forum and jurisdiction and that would be the basis for determining revisional forum." 

 34. In view of the larger Bench decision quoted above, we are of the view that since the revisional application arises out of title Suit No. 407 of 2005 which was valued at Taka 2,57,01,000 and exceeds pecuniary jurisdiction of Taka 5,00,000 of the District Judge in which the District Judge has no appellate Jurisdiction. Hence Civil Revision No. 21 of 2006 before the learned District Judge or Additional District Judge Court is not maintainable. 

 35. The question of jurisdiction of the court has to be decided at the earliest opportunity and referred to section 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure which is in the following terms: 

 "Save insofar as is otherwise expressly provided nothing herein contained shall operate to give any court’s jurisdiction over suits the amount or value of the subject matter of which exceeds the pecuniary limits (if any) of its ordinary jurisdiction." 

 36. We observed that since the suit is valued at much above Taka 5 lac then the revisional application can only be disposed of by a court which has got the necessary pecuniary jurisdiction. The District Judge cannot entertain any revisional application under section 115(2) of the Code beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction which is fixed at Taka 5,00,000 being the appellate Jurisdiction. The relevant provision of the Civil Courts Act, 1887 and the provision of Code of Civil Procedure observed that the court which is not invested with appellate power cannot also exercise revisional power. 

 38. In view of the provision of section 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure and section 115(2) of the Code expressed the view that civil revision against an order of Joint District Judge in a suit or proceeding pending before it the value of the subject matter of which is above and beyond Taka 5,00,000 being the pecuniary jurisdiction of District Judge can never be preferred in the court of District Judge. 

 40. In view of our above discussion, the question No. 1 as formulated by us as to whether the District Judge has unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction in entertaining revisional application, is found in the negative. The District Judge has no unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction in entertaining revisional application under section 115(2) of the Code. Second question as regard the error of the impugned order is answered in the affirmative. The Additional District Judge committed an error in passing the impugned order dated 29-3-2006. 

 41. In view of above discussion, we are of the view that this revisional application has merit. The plaintiffs-opposite parties-petitioners are entitled to get relief.
